lead.headline: Personal Computers Move Deeper Into Everyday Office Work
lead.summary: By mid-1986, the IBM-compatible PC had become the practical business default while Macintosh, Amiga, Atari ST, and Commodore machines kept the home and creative markets lively.

computerItems.label: Hardware
computerItems.headline: 80286 PCs and Hard Disks Push the Office Past the Hobby Era
computerItems.summary: Faster IBM-compatible systems, falling storage costs, and common business peripherals made the desktop computer feel less experimental and more like office infrastructure.

computerItems.label: Software
computerItems.headline: Spreadsheets, Databases, and Word Processors Define the Workday
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3, dBASE, WordPerfect, and DOS utilities remained the practical software stack for many small offices.

computerItems.label: Games
computerItems.headline: Adventure Games, Commodore 64 Titles, and Console Imports Fill Store Shelves
computerItems.summary: Computer-game coverage in 1986 was scattered across magazine issues and store availability, so daily entries should separate exact releases from reviews and shelf reports.

computerItems.label: Online
computerItems.headline: Modems and Bulletin Board Systems Bring Home Users Onto Phone Lines
computerItems.summary: BBS culture was becoming a real part of hobby computing, with 300- and 1200-baud modems turning isolated machines into local communities.
